claims.claim: A loaded Boeing 747-400 can weigh up to about 400 tonnes
claims.definition: Maximum take-off weight (MTOW) class of the 747-400: approximately 396,890 kg (875,000 lb), i.e. just under 400 t; 'loaded up to 400 tonnes' refers to the MTOW class, not every departure weight.
claims.authoritative_source: Boeing 747-400 airplane characteristics; NASA Glenn Research Center educational pages
sources: Boeing 747-400 airplane characteristics for airport planning
NASA Glenn educational 'Beginner's Guide to Aeronautics'
claims.notes: Rounded to 400 t for narration; MTOW is a certification figure, stable for the type.

claims.claim: Flow that accelerates over a curved surface sits at lower static pressure (Bernoulli principle)
claims.definition: Along a streamline of incompressible flow, an increase in speed coincides with a drop in static pressure. Lift is best described as a pressure difference integrated over the airfoil surface; the curvature/turning of the flow is the physical cause.
claims.measured_value: qualitative relationship: faster flow -> lower static pressure
claims.authoritative_source: NASA Glenn Research Center, 'Bernoulli and Newton' (Beginner's Guide to Aeronautics); Anderson, 'Fundamentals of Aerodynamics'
sources: NASA Glenn Beginner's Guide to Aeronautics

claims.claim: A lifting wing deflects air downward (downwash) and the equal-and-opposite reaction acts upward on the wing
claims.definition: Newton's third law applied to a lifting surface: the wing turns the airflow downward; the momentum change corresponds to an upward force on the wing. Same physical lift as the pressure-integral description, told from the momentum side.
claims.measured_value: qualitative: downwash momentum flux balances lift
claims.authoritative_source: NASA Glenn Research Center, 'Newton's Third Law of Motion' (Beginner's Guide to Aeronautics)
sources: NASA Glenn Beginner's Guide to Aeronautics

claims.claim: Beyond a critical angle of attack the flow separates and lift collapses (stall)
claims.definition: As nose-up angle grows, lift rises roughly linearly until a critical angle of attack (of order 15 degrees for a clean transport wing); beyond it the boundary layer separates, the attached-flow pattern breaks down and lift drops sharply.
claims.measured_value: critical angle of attack of order 15 degrees (clean wing)
claims.authoritative_source: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (stall chapter); Anderson, 'Fundamentals of Aerodynamics'
sources: FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge
